name: Kabuki Syndrome

criteria.description: Distinctive facial features including long palpebral fissures with eversion of the lateral third of the lower eyelid, arched eyebrows with sparse lateral third, and prominent ears
Skeletal anomalies such as brachydactyly, clinodactyly, and vertebral abnormalities
Mild to moderate intellectual disability or developmental delay
Postnatal growth deficiency or short stature
Pathogenic mutation in KMT2D or KDM6A genes

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of all three major criteria (distinctive facial features, skeletal anomalies, intellectual disability) or genetic confirmation with supportive clinical features
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Genetic testing is increasingly used to confirm diagnosis; clinical diagnosis remains important in resource-limited settings.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Long palpebral fissures with eversion of lateral lower eyelid
searchTerms: long eye openings with outward lower eyelid
wide palpebral fissures with eyelid eversion
large eye openings with eyelid turning out

pathognomonic.symptomName: Arched eyebrows with sparse lateral third
searchTerms: arched eyebrows with thin outer third
high curved eyebrows with hair loss laterally

pathognomonic.symptomName: Prominent large ears with fleshy lobes
searchTerms: large prominent ears with thick lobes

common.symptomName: Skeletal anomalies including brachydactyly and clinodactyly

searchTerms: heart defects like holes in septum

occasional.symptomName: Cleft palate or submucous cleft palate
occasional.notes: May cause feeding and speech difficulties
searchTerms: split or incomplete roof of mouth

rare.notes: Reported in a minority of cases
searchTerms: mental health and social interaction problems

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests; possible immunoglobulin abnormalities
Thyroid function tests may reveal hypothyroidism
imaging: Skeletal X-rays showing brachydactyly, vertebral anomalies
genetic: Pathogenic variants in KMT2D (majority of cases)

distinguishingFeatures: Distinct facial features different from Kabuki syndrome
Characteristic ear anomalies distinct from Kabuki syndrome

redFlags: Severe congenital heart defects requiring early intervention
references: Niikawa N, et al. Kabuki make-up syndrome: a syndrome of mental retardation, unusual facies, large and protruding ears, and postnatal growth deficiency. J Pediatr. 1981.
Adam MP, et al. Kabuki syndrome. GeneReviews. 2020.
Miyake N, et al. KMT2D mutations in Kabuki syndrome. Nat Genet. 2013.
commonPitfalls: Facial features may be subtle in infancy and missed without longitudinal follow-up.
Developmental delay may be attributed to non-syndromic causes if dysmorphic features are overlooked.
Congenital heart defects may lead to misdiagnosis as other syndromic or isolated cardiac conditions.
Hypotonia and joint laxity may be mistaken for benign joint hypermobility or other connective tissue disorders.

extendedDiscriminators.feature: Arched eyebrows with sparse lateral third, long palpebral fissures, and eversion of the lower eyelid are more characteristic of Kabuki syndrome.
Persistent fingertip pads and skeletal anomalies (e.g., brachydactyly, vertebral anomalies) are more typical of Kabuki syndrome, while coloboma and choanal atresia are hallmarks of CHARGE.
Kabuki syndrome lacks the 'elfin' facies and supravalvular aortic stenosis seen in Williams syndrome, and instead has distinctive facial features and persistent fingertip pads.

ruleOutCriteria: Absence of characteristic facial features (arched eyebrows, long palpebral fissures, eversion of lower eyelid) in a patient with developmental delay and congenital anomalies.
Molecular genetic testing negative for pathogenic variants in KMT2D or KDM6A in a patient with classic clinical features.
Presence of major diagnostic features of another syndrome (e.g., coloboma and choanal atresia of CHARGE syndrome) without features of Kabuki syndrome.
